Stage 1 · Warm-up

Telling it like it happened

Everybody has one journey they can still tell ten years later. Usually it is the one that went wrong.

1 · Read the explanation.
Which tense carries which job

A spoken story runs on the past simple. Every event that moves the story forward takes it, in the order the events happened. The past continuous paints whatever was already going on around those events. The past perfect does something different: it reaches back behind the point you have reached, without stopping the story to explain.

The same event can take either form. I parked in an empty car park is the event as it happens. I had parked in a school playground is the same act seen from the following morning — and the whole joke depends on that shift.

Three places the past perfect earns its place
  • Setting up. What was already arranged before the story starts: we had booked a campsite.
  • Explaining. A reason that lies earlier than the moment you are describing: there had been an accident ahead of us.
  • Looking back. The story reaches a point, and you show the character realising what they had done: you know what I’d done?

Everywhere else, use the past simple. If two events are told in the order they happened and joined by and, so or then, no past perfect is needed at all.

Two things to watch

1 — The past perfect is a tool, not a level. Using it for every past event does not make your English more advanced; it makes the story impossible to follow, because nothing seems to be happening now.

2 — A story needs a listener. In both recordings the teller stops repeatedly and the listener supplies you’re kidding, that’s hilarious, I bet you were furious. When you write a story down you lose those, so the writing has to do their work instead.

10 · Read this before the extra practice.
One story, two clocks

The past simple is the clock that moves: I saw a car park and parked there. Every new past simple verb advances the story. The past perfect is the clock that stays where it is and looks backwards from that point: We had booked into a campsite outside Paris · There had been an accident on the motorway. Reaching back does not stop the story; that is the whole point of the form.

Two extensions carry a great deal of a travel narrative. The passive reports what was done to you before the story reached that point, when the doer is irrelevant: The flight had been cancelled · My luggage had been sent to the wrong airport. The continuous gives the length of something up to that point, and is the natural way to explain a state: We had been camping for a fortnight · I was exhausted, because I had been driving since four.

Choosing, sentence by sentence

Ask two questions of each verb. First: is this event on the main line of the story, or off it? Events on the line take the past simple; things that were merely going on take the past continuous (Liz was reading the map, The children were sleeping in the back). Second: does it belong to an earlier moment than the one I am describing? If so, the past perfect.

Keep the punchline structure in mind, because it is the most useful pattern in the lesson: You know what I had done? I had parked in a school playground. The story stands still and the reader is shown what was already true. The negative version does the same work: Nobody had told us the road was closed.

And, as in lesson 11: when then, before, after or by the time is doing the ordering, do not double up. I got up, then I opened the door needs no past perfect; By the time I reached the desk, the flight had gone does.

Errors to watch: The flight had cancelled → had been cancelled · We had camped for a fortnight and were filthy → had been camping · I got up and had opened the door → opened.

6 · Now write the letter of complaint.

You booked a weekend painting course. It was cancelled after you had arrived, and nobody had told you. Write to the school. 150–180 words.

Include
  • Dear Sir or Madam and, at the end, Yours faithfully;
  • a first line saying what you are writing about and when it happened;
  • the events in order, in the past simple;
  • at least three past perfect forms, one of them passive;
  • one sentence saying what was inconvenient rather than exaggerating it;
  • a clear request for compensation, and what you expect;
  • at least five items from stage 2, and no informal reactions.

4 · Read the model.
Model · a letter of complaint

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing about the mixed media weekend of 14–15 March, which I had booked in January, and to request compensation for the way it was handled.

I travelled down from Leeds on the Friday evening. My train was delayed by an hour because a lorry had turned over on the line near Bristol, so I reached the guest house at midnight. On the Saturday morning I arrived at the studio at 9.45 and found a notice on the door. The course had been cancelled two days earlier. Nobody had contacted me, although you hold both my email address and my telephone number.

I understand that a tutor may fall ill at short notice. What I do not understand is why I was not told. The cancellation itself was inconvenient; travelling four hundred miles to read about it on a door was not.

I should therefore be grateful if you would refund the course fee in full and cover my travel and one night’s accommodation, which came to £186. I enclose copies of both receipts and look forward to your reply within fourteen days.

Yours faithfully,
